text: The Born rule tells you the probability of each measurement outcome, but not what happens to the qubit the instant after you measure. The answer is both simple and drastic: the superposition is gone, permanently.

Suppose a qubit is in superposition and you measure it. The Born rule only gives you the probability of each outcome — collapse is a separate postulate describing what happens next. If the outcome is 0, the qubit's state immediately becomes exactly ket-zero — not mostly ket-zero, not a weaker version of the original superposition, just exactly ket-zero. Measure the same qubit again right away, with no gates in between, and you're guaranteed to get 0 again — the randomness was a one-time event, already resolved.

Here's the part that trips people up: collapse is irreversible and destroys information. Before measuring, the qubit's amplitudes encoded a rich, continuous description — magnitude and relative phase. After collapsing to, say, ket-zero, all of that is gone, and you cannot work backward to recover what those amplitudes originally were. There's no gate, no clever trick, no post-processing that undoes a measurement and hands back the original superposition.

This is the single most important practical consequence for writing quantum software: you cannot measure a qubit partway through a circuit just to check on it and keep going as if nothing happened. The instant you measure, you collapse it out of whatever superposition the earlier gates built, and that information is gone. That's exactly why algorithms build the full superposition through an uninterrupted sequence of gates and measure only once, at the end. This irreversibility also previews chapter 5's no-cloning theorem: if you could duplicate a qubit first, you could measure the copy and keep the original untouched — dodging collapse entirely. Nature forbids that too.
Next lesson shows that the computational basis is just one choice among many — and that which basis you measure in is itself a real, physically consequential decision.
